questions.prompt: A CI job clones a repository whose working tree is 40 MB, yet the clone downloads 2.3 GB. What explains it?
choices: The server sends the working tree uncompressed
Git also downloads every developer's reflog
A clone transfers every object reachable from the wanted refs, so every version of every file ever committed is in the pack, including large files deleted years ago
HTTP cannot compress binary data
questions.explanation: The server packs history, not a snapshot. A file deleted in a later commit is still reachable from the commits before that, so it stays in every full clone until history is rewritten. A shallow or partial clone asks for less; LFS keeps such files out of the object graph in the first place.

questions.prompt: `git verify-pack -v` prints `f8762335... blob 7 18 5502 1 7972c09a...` for a file of about 7 KB. Why is the size column 7?
choices: For a deltified entry the size column is the size of the delta instructions; the blob is rebuilt from base 7972c09a by copy and insert instructions, and 1 is its chain depth
The blob is truncated and git fsck will report it
Sizes in verify-pack are in kilobytes
7 is the compressed size and 18 the uncompressed size
questions.explanation: The size in a pack entry header is the size of the entry's inflated data. For OFS_DELTA and REF_DELTA entries that data is the delta: two size varints and a few copy and insert opcodes. 18 is the entry's size in the pack, header and zlib stream included.

questions.prompt: `git clone --filter=blob:none` against your company's Git server ends up as a full clone, and stderr shows `warning: filtering not recognized by server, ignoring`. What do you change?
choices: Add --depth 1 so the filter is applied
Force protocol.version=0 on the client
Upgrade the client, which is too old to send filters
Set uploadpack.allowFilter=true on the served repository (or the hosting product's equivalent): without it the server does not list filter in its fetch capability and the client drops the argument
questions.explanation: Filters are a server feature. The capability advertisement says fetch=shallow wait-for-done without filter, so the client never sends the filter line and the server packs every blob. minipack's clone prints the same warning for the same reason.

questions.prompt: In a smart-HTTP fetch negotiation, why does the second POST repeat all the want lines and the haves the server already ACKed?
choices: To defeat HTTP caching between the client and the server

Each POST is answered by a fresh upload-pack process that remembers nothing from the previous request, so the client restates the state that matters: what it wants and which commits are known to be common
Because pkt-lines can be lost on the wire and must be retransmitted
The server requires every request to be signed with the full want list
questions.explanation: Over HTTP the protocol is stateless. Over SSH or git:// one upload-pack process lives for the whole conversation, but each HTTP request starts a new one, so wants and common haves travel again in every round until done or ready.

questions.prompt: A release job in a `--depth 1` clone runs `git describe --tags` and fails with `No names found`, although the repository has tags. Which fix addresses the mechanism?
choices: Run git gc before describe
Delete .git/shallow so Git stops treating the clone as shallow

Fetch the history the tag sits on, for example `git fetch --unshallow --tags` or `fetch-depth: 0` in actions/checkout: the tagged commit is below the shallow boundary, so neither it nor the tag was fetched
Set protocol.version=1
questions.explanation: Depth 1 implies a single branch and tag following, which only brings tags that point into the fetched commits. Deleting .git/shallow does not fetch anything; it makes Git look for parents that are not there, so fsck and log fail. A blob-less partial clone keeps every commit and tag and is often the better choice for such jobs.

questions.prompt: A repository holds 30 versions of a 200 MB compressed video. Why does Git LFS help where `git gc --aggressive` does not?
choices: Compressed media changes almost completely between versions, so the delta search finds no shared blocks and every version is stored whole in every full clone; LFS replaces the blob with a small pointer and downloads only the versions a checkout needs from a separate store
LFS compresses video better than zlib does
gc --aggressive deletes old versions of large files
LFS stores large files in .git/shallow so they are skipped
questions.explanation: gc --aggressive only widens the delta window and lengthens chains; it cannot find copy instructions where none exist, and it never removes reachable objects. LFS changes what is in the object graph: a pointer of about 130 bytes per version instead of the content.
